patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent severe episodic abdominal pain with progressive neuropathy and psychiatric symptoms over 18 months
patient.history_present_illness: Marcus Chen is a 35-year-old junior attorney presenting for neurological evaluation after 18 months of recurrent severe episodic abdominal pain, peripheral neuropathy, and intermittent psychiatric symptoms. His illness began with 3 episodes of severe colicky diffuse abdominal pain lasting 2-5 days each (first 12 months), requiring emergency room visits; imaging (CT abdomen) was consistently normal and he was told to follow up with gastroenterology. He was worked up for appendicitis, bowel obstruction, and renal colic — all negative. Gastroenterology attributed the pain to 'functional abdominal pain' or irritable bowel syndrome, but he strongly disputes this given the severity. Three months ago, he developed progressive bilateral leg weakness and sensory loss, and one month ago experienced a transient 3-day episode of confusion and disorientation (resolved spontaneously). He reports that the neuropathy episodes seem temporally related to the abdominal pain crises. He was on no psychiatric medications but was seen by psychiatry who documented 'unclear anxiety disorder with somatization' after his first confusion episode. He has noted dark discoloration of his urine during the abdominal episodes ('like port wine'). He is an attorney and has been under significant stress, attributed by multiple physicians as the cause. He takes no medications, does not drink alcohol, does not use illicit drugs, and has no relevant family history — though his maternal cousin had 'some rare blood disorder that caused seizures' (details unknown). He has not been exposed to toxins. He fasted extensively (24-hour fasts, 2-3x/month as part of an intermittent fasting regimen that he has maintained for 2 years).

specialized_test.impression: ABNORMAL NCS/EMG — acute motor-predominant axonal polyneuropathy, proximal greater than distal. Motor nerve amplitudes markedly reduced bilaterally in proximal-predominant distribution; sensory nerve action potentials reduced but relatively less affected. Conduction velocities relatively preserved. EMG: widespread active denervation (fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves) in proximal and distal muscles bilaterally. Recruitment markedly reduced. Findings indicate an acute axonal neuropathy with a proximal predominance, atypical for length-dependent diabetic or toxic neuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.query: acute intermittent porphyria drug precipitants unsafe medications list

results.citation: European Porphyria Network EPNET Drug Database 2024 (drugs-porphyria.eu)
results.summary: UNSAFE drugs in acute porphyria (partial list): Barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate (anticonvulsants — almost all are unsafe), alcohol, oral contraceptives, progesterone, sulfonamides, rifampin, griseofulvin, trimethoprim, ergots, ketamine. SAFE analgesics for porphyric pain: morphine, fentanyl, opioids (safe), acetaminophen (safe), NSAIDs (generally safe). Gabapentin is generally considered safe. Benzodiazepines are SAFE (important for agitation/seizure management). Beta-blockers are SAFE (heart rate/BP management in autonomic crisis).

output.summary: Published databases document a large number of medications with porphyrinogenic risk in acute porphyria (partial list summarized in results above). Population-level evidence on drug safety classifications for AIP summarized above. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.query: givosiran AIP prevention recurrent attacks siRNA

results.citation: Balwani M et al. (2020) Phase 3 trial of RNAi therapeutic givosiran for acute intermittent porphyria. NEJM 382:2289-2301.
results.summary: Givosiran (siRNA targeting hepatic ALAS1 mRNA) reduces AIP attack rate by 74% vs placebo. SC injection monthly. FDA-approved for recurrent AIP attacks. Normalizes urinary ALA/PBG in most patients. Side effects: injection site reactions, nausea, hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs). Improves neuropathy outcomes by preventing recurrent porphyric neurological crises.

output.summary: Published phase 3 trial data demonstrate givosiran reduces AIP attack rate by approximately 74% versus placebo in patients with recurrent attacks. Mechanism, dosing schedule, and side effect profile summarized in results above. Population-level outcomes on neuropathy progression and urinary ALA/PBG normalization summarized above. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) with porphyric polyneuropathy (HMBS variant)

differential.key_features: Motor-predominant, abdominal pain, basophilic stippling; need blood/urine heavy metal panel.
Acute motor axonal; areflexia, monophasic; CSF albuminocytologic dissociation; relevant if rapidly ascending.
Multiple ER visits with negative imaging anchor here; but objective NCS abnormalities argue otherwise.
Demyelinating, chronic relapsing pattern; less explosive than porphyric crisis.
Asymmetric multifocal axonal; need ANCA / ANA / biopsy.

optimal_actions.action: Order broad neuropathy labs (CBC, CMP, HbA1c, B12 + MMA, TSH, SPEP/IFE, urinalysis)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify reversible/treatable etiologies (diabetes, B12 deficiency, monoclonal gammopathy, thyroid disease)

optimal_actions.action: Order EMG/NCS to characterize axonal vs demyelinating pattern and distribution
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Length-dependent axonal vs demyelinating vs multifocal pattern; severity and distribution

optimal_actions.action: Search literature for DSP evaluation guidelines and etiology-specific recommendations
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirm AAN 2009 DSP workup, etiology-specific evaluations

optimal_actions.action: Review medications for neurotoxic agents and check interactions for symptomatic therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify potentially neurotoxic drugs (chemotherapy, metronidazole, megadose B6, nitrofurantoin); guide neuropathic-pain pharmacotherapy

optimal_actions.action: Spot urine porphobilinogen (PBG), δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), total porphyrins, and quantification on a freshly-voided light-protected sample during an attack
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Markedly elevated urine PBG and ALA during attack confirm acute hepatic porphyria

optimal_actions.action: Targeted porphyria gene panel (HMBS, ALAS1, CPOX, PPOX) when biochemistry positive
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Pathogenic variant in HMBS confirms acute intermittent porphyria

optimal_actions.action: Heavy metal screen (lead, arsenic, thallium) — porphyric crisis differential and lead inhibits ALAD
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Rule out lead poisoning (mimics porphyric crisis and elevates ALA)

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is a cortical test and is non-contributory in peripheral nerve disease.
Head/brain CT has no role in peripheral neuropathy evaluation.
Brain MRI is not indicated in typical distal symmetric polyneuropathy without CNS signs.
Advanced cerebral imaging (PET/MRA/MRV/perfusion) has no routine role in peripheral neuropathy.
Echocardiography is not indicated unless cardiac amyloid is suspected.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated unless there is syncope or symptomatic dysautonomia with arrhythmia concern.

sequence_constraints.reason: Tier the workup — basic labs first, then targeted electrodiagnostic and tissue studies.

critical_actions: Recognize acute motor-predominant axonal neuropathy + recurrent abdominal pain + psychiatric symptoms = porphyric crisis
Obtain spot urine PBG and ALA on a fresh, light-protected sample DURING the attack (key timing)
Heavy metal screen to exclude lead poisoning
Treat with IV hemin (heme arginate or Panhematin), high-dose glucose, and pain control with safe agents
Avoid porphyrinogenic drugs (barbiturates, sulfonamides, valproate, oral contraceptives, rifampin, etc.)
contraindicated_actions: Do not give porphyrinogenic medications (barbiturates, sulfonamides, valproate, rifampin, OCPs, ergots)
Do not dismiss as IBS or anxiety without checking urine PBG during an attack
key_reasoning_points: The triad of abdominal pain + neuropsychiatric symptoms + motor neuropathy is the classic porphyric crisis
Diagnosis requires urine PBG/ALA testing DURING an attack (light-protected, fresh)
HMBS gene confirmation supports family screening and trigger avoidance counseling

red_herrings.data_point: Multiple negative ER imaging studies for abdominal pain
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Recurrent unexplained severe abdominal pain with neurologic and psychiatric features = porphyric crisis until proven otherwise.
